subjects.title: CCAF 6 - Exam Scenarios
subjects.description: End-to-end architecture sketches for the six exam scenarios, plus the design decisions each one tests.

cards.question: Scenario 1 - Customer Support Agent. Sketch the end-to-end architecture.
cards.answer:
**Shape**: routing -> agentic loop with tools -> escalation.

- **Router** classifies the ticket (billing / technical / account) and picks a specialized system prompt; easy high-volume categories go to a smaller model.
- **System prompt** (cached prefix): role, tone, policy, escalation rules, output contract. **User turn**: this customer's message.
- **Tools**: `get_order`, `get_account`, `search_kb` (read), `issue_refund`, `create_ticket` (write, gated), `escalate_to_human`.
- **Knowledge base** through an MCP server, so the same tools serve the web widget and the internal agent console.
- **Loop**: branch on `stop_reason`; execute tools; return `tool_result` (with `is_error: true` on failure); repeat.
- **Escalation** is a **tool**, not a phrase - triggered by low confidence, policy categories, a refund above the threshold, repeated tool failures, or the user asking for a human.
- **State**: conversation persisted per session; order/account state stays in your DB and is reached through tools.
- **Guardrails**: the refund threshold is enforced **in code**, never by prompt.
- **Reliability**: retry 429/5xx with backoff, fall back to a smaller model, degrade to "a specialist will follow up" plus a ticket.
- **Observability**: containment rate, escalation rate, tool error rate, cost per conversation.
hints: Start with the router, end with escalation - and remember where the refund threshold has to live.

cards.question: Scenario 2 - Multi-Agent Research Pipeline. Sketch the end-to-end architecture.
cards.answer:
**Shape**: orchestrator-workers, then synthesis, then verification.

- **Orchestrator** decomposes the question at runtime into sub-questions (the decomposition depends on the question - this is what makes it orchestrator-workers, not sectioning).
- **Workers** run **in parallel**, each with its own context window, a **read-only** tool set (search, fetch, read), and a self-contained brief - a subagent inherits no memory of the parent conversation.
- **Workers return compact structured summaries**, with citations - never raw pages. This is what keeps the orchestrator's context from exploding.
- **Synthesis** merges findings, resolves contradictions, and flags gaps.
- **Verification** pass: independent checkers try to **refute** each claim; a claim survives only with support. Perspective diversity beats repeating the same check.
- **Context**: key summary at the top, tool outputs trimmed at the source, orchestrator history compacted at a threshold.
- **Caching**: the shared research system prompt and tool definitions sit in the cached prefix reused by every worker.
- **Termination**: `stop_reason`, plus a per-worker circuit breaker that escalates rather than returning partial findings as complete.
- **Cost control**: cap workers per run and depth per worker; log what was dropped instead of silently truncating coverage.

The pipeline:

```mermaid
graph TD
  Q["Question"] --> O["Orchestrator decomposes at runtime"]
  O --> W1["Worker: own context, read-only tools"]
  O --> W2["Worker: own context, read-only tools"]
  O --> W3["Worker: own context, read-only tools"]
  W1 -->|compact summary with citations| S["Synthesis: merge, resolve contradictions, flag gaps"]
  W2 -->|compact summary with citations| S
  W3 -->|compact summary with citations| S
  S --> V["Verification: independent checkers try to refute each claim"]
  V --> R["Answer, only claims that survived"]
```
hints: Runtime decomposition, parallel read-only workers, and one rule about what they hand back.

cards.question: Scenario 3 - CI/CD Integration. Sketch the end-to-end architecture.
cards.answer:
**Shape**: Claude Code in headless mode inside the pipeline, with configuration in version control.

- **Trigger**: `@claude` mentions on issues/PRs via the GitHub app for interactive work; a plain workflow step running `claude -p` for checks that must run on **every** PR.
- **Invocation**: `claude -p "<task>" --output-format json --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Bash(git diff:*)"` so a downstream step can parse the result.
- **Configuration in the repo**: `CLAUDE.md` (conventions - the only way a CI agent learns them, since no human corrects it mid-run), `.claude/settings.json` (permissions, hooks), `.claude/commands/` (the review command), `.mcp.json` (shared servers).
- **Permissions**: explicit allow list; `deny` on secrets and infra paths. **Never** `--dangerously-skip-permissions` on a repo with real credentials - CI content (issue text, dependency files) is untrusted input that can carry injected instructions.
- **Secrets**: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in repository secrets, referenced from the workflow; job `permissions` scoped to `contents`/`pull-requests`/`issues`.
- **Hooks** for deterministic steps: `PostToolUse` to format after edits, `PreToolUse` to block protected paths.
- **Guardrails**: Claude proposes a branch/PR; merging stays a human decision.
- **Observability**: cost per run (from the JSON output), pass/fail rate, and how often the review's findings are acted on.
hints: Headless in the pipeline, configuration in the repo, and untrusted content everywhere.

cards.question: Scenario 4 - Structured Data Extraction. Sketch the end-to-end architecture.
cards.answer:
**Shape**: a workflow, not an agent - the steps are known in advance.

- **Prompt layout**: document **first** inside `<document>` tags with a source and index; instructions and the question **last** (long data at the top, query at the end).
- **Contract**: a tool whose `input_schema` is the target schema, forced with `tool_choice`. Enums for closed sets, `null` allowed for absent fields, plus a `confidence` or `needs_review` field.
- **Grounding**: require the model to quote the source passage before extracting, which suppresses invention on long documents.
- **Chunking** for documents beyond the window: split with overlap, extract per chunk, merge and de-duplicate in code. Chunk boundaries are a correctness risk - a table split in half loses rows.
- **Sampling**: `temperature: 0`.
- **Caching**: instructions, schema, and few-shot examples in the stable prefix; only the document varies.
- **Validation in code**: schema check, business rules (line items sum to the total), and route failures + low confidence to human review rather than into the database.
- **Scale**: batch processing for bulk backfills; retry 429/5xx with backoff and jitter.
- **Monitoring**: field-level accuracy, `needs_review` rate, and rejected-record rate against a labeled gold set.

The flow, including the chunking branch:

```mermaid
graph TD
  D["Document"] --> F{"Fits the context window?"}
  F -->|yes| E["Extract once"]
  F -->|no| C["Split into chunks, with overlap"]
  C --> EC["Extract per chunk"]
  EC --> M["Merge and de-duplicate in code"]
  E --> V["Validate against the forced tool schema"]
  M --> V
  V --> N{"needs_review, or low confidence?"}
  N -->|yes| H["Human review queue"]
  N -->|no| OUT["Accepted records"]
```
hints: The steps are known in advance - so this is not an agent. Document first, contract second.

cards.question: Support agent scenario: the agent must never promise a refund above $500 without approval. Where does the rule belong?
cards.answer: In the tool implementation. The model proposes; your code decides whether it executes. A prompt instruction or a schema `maximum` shapes behavior but does not enforce policy.

choices.text: Enforced in the `issue_refund` tool implementation, which routes anything over $500 to approval
In the system prompt as a hard rule
As `maximum: 500` in the tool's JSON schema
In a CLAUDE.md file for the project

hints: Which of these is enforcement, and which are polite requests?

cards.question: Support agent scenario: conversations run 30+ turns and cost is climbing. Which change helps most, with no quality loss?
cards.answer: Cache the stable prefix. The system prompt, policy, examples, and tool definitions are resent on every turn; cache reads cost about a tenth of base input, so this is usually the single biggest lever in a multi-turn agent.

choices.text: Add a `cache_control` breakpoint after the system prompt and tool definitions
Reduce `max_tokens` so replies are shorter
Drop the oldest turns from history on every request
Disable tools for turns that look like small talk

hints: What is being re-sent, unchanged, on every one of those 30 turns?

cards.question: Research pipeline scenario: workers return full page text and the orchestrator hits its context limit. Best fix?
cards.answer: Have each worker return a compact structured summary with citations. Context isolation is the reason subagents exist - the worker absorbs the bulk reading and hands back only the distilled result.

choices.text: Have each worker return a compact structured summary with citations
Run the workers sequentially so results arrive spread out
Move to a model with a larger context window
Increase the orchestrator's `max_tokens`

hints: Why do subagents exist in the first place?

cards.question: Research pipeline scenario: findings must be trustworthy. Which verification design is strongest?
cards.answer: Independent verifiers prompted to refute, each with a distinct lens, catch failure modes that redundant identical checks miss. Asking the same agent to re-read its own work is the weakest option.

choices.text: Independent verifiers, each with a different lens, prompted to refute each claim
Ask the synthesizing agent to double-check its own output
Raise the thinking budget on the orchestrator
Set temperature to 0 on every worker

hints: Independence and disagreement are the point - self-review is not.

cards.question: CI/CD scenario: a review must run automatically on every PR and produce output a later step consumes. What do you use?
cards.answer: Headless mode with `--output-format json` runs unattended on every PR and emits a structured result. The `@claude` mention flow requires a human to write a comment.

choices.text: `claude -p` in a workflow step with `--output-format json` and an explicit `--allowedTools` list
A bot that posts `@claude review this` on each PR
An interactive session on a self-hosted runner
A scheduled job that opens the repo in the desktop app

hints: "Automatically on every PR" rules out anything a human has to trigger.

cards.question: CI/CD scenario: the CI agent keeps violating team conventions that a human would normally correct in chat. What fixes it?
cards.answer: Commit the conventions to `CLAUDE.md`. In CI there is no human to correct the agent mid-run, so repository instructions are the only channel for project context - and anything that must be guaranteed goes in hooks or permissions instead.

choices.text: Put the conventions in the repository `CLAUDE.md`, and enforce the non-negotiable ones with hooks
Add the conventions to each workflow step's prompt string
Raise the model tier for CI runs
Enable `--dangerously-skip-permissions` so the agent is not interrupted

hints: In CI nobody corrects the agent mid-run. Where do conventions have to live?

cards.question: Extraction scenario: documents exceed the context window. What is the correct approach?
cards.answer: Chunk with overlap, extract per chunk against the same schema, then merge and de-duplicate in code. Overlap and code-side merging are what protect records that straddle a boundary.

choices.text: Chunk with overlap, extract per chunk with the same schema, merge and de-duplicate in code
Truncate each document to the window size
Summarize the document first, then extract from the summary
Split at exact window boundaries with no overlap

hints: What protects a record that straddles a chunk boundary?

cards.question: Extraction scenario: which design most reduces bad records reaching the database?
cards.answer: Schema-forced output plus code-side validation plus a confidence field routing uncertain records to human review. Each layer catches what the previous one misses; none of them alone is sufficient.

choices.text: Forced tool schema, business-rule validation in code, and a confidence field that routes uncertain records to review
A strongly worded instruction to be accurate
Extended thinking with a large budget on every document
Running each extraction twice and keeping the longer result

hints: No single layer is enough - look for the option that stacks several.

cards.question: Monitoring scenario: the triage agent's log tool returns 10,000 lines per call. What breaks and what is the fix?
cards.answer: Context is exhausted and the useful signal lands in the middle of a huge blob, where attention is weakest. Fix it at the source: filter and aggregate server-side, return the relevant window with counts.

choices.text: Context exhaustion and lost-in-the-middle - filter and aggregate in the tool, return a relevant window
Nothing breaks if the model has a large context window
Rate limits - reduce the polling interval
Only cost - enable caching on the log output

hints: Two problems at once: the window fills, and the signal lands in the worst position.

cards.question: Support scenario: the agent must handle a question outside its domain. What is the best-designed behavior?
cards.answer: Define the out-of-scope path explicitly - say it is out of scope and hand off through the escalation tool. An undefined out-of-scope behavior is where agents improvise confidently and cause harm.

choices.text: State it is out of scope and call the escalation tool with the context gathered so far
Answer as best it can from general knowledge
Return an empty response
Loop until it finds a tool that seems related

hints: Undefined out-of-scope behavior is where agents improvise confidently.

cards.question: Across all six scenarios, which single question most often decides the correct exam answer?
cards.answer: "Is this enforced by code or merely suggested to the model?" Policy, authorization, thresholds, and termination must live in code; the model contributes judgment and language. Nearly every distractor in these scenarios is a prompt-level substitute for a code-level control.

choices.text: Is the constraint enforced in code, or only suggested to the model?
Which model tier is being used?
Is the temperature set to 0?
Is the context window large enough?

hints: Look at what almost every wrong option in this deck has in common.

cards.question: Match each exam scenario to the orchestration pattern it most naturally uses.
cards.answer: Recognizing the pattern from the scenario framing is most of the work - once the pattern is right, the tooling, context, and reliability answers usually follow.

matchPairs.right: Workflow (prompt chain) with a forced tool schema
Parallel sectioning + voting on the policy check
Deterministic detection + LLM triage + gated remediation

hints: Ask for each: are the steps known in advance, and who decides the decomposition?

cards.question: Match each scenario to the failure mode it is most likely to be tested on.
cards.answer:
Each scenario has a signature trap, and that is what the question is really testing. Knowing the pairing turns four plausible-looking options into one.

| Scenario | Signature trap | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| Customer support | Policy enforced by prompt instead of by code | Refund limits and escalation rules are business rules; a prompt is context, not an enforcement layer |
| Research pipeline | Worker output floods the orchestrator's context | Parallel workers each produce a lot; if they return raw pages the orchestrator drowns in its own subagents |
| CI/CD | Over-broad permissions on untrusted repository content | The agent runs against code a stranger opened a PR with, so its permissions are the blast radius |
| Data extraction | Invented values for fields missing from the source | Asked for a field that is not in the document, a model would rather fill it than leave it empty |
| Monitoring | Irreversible remediation taken without a human gate | Detection is cheap to get wrong; acting on a wrong detection is what costs you |

The through-line: not one of these is fixed by a better prompt. Each needs something your code owns - a schema that allows `null`, a permission scope, an approval gate before an irreversible action, a brief telling workers to return summaries.

matchPairs.right: Policy enforced by prompt instead of by code
Worker output floods the orchestrator's context
Over-broad permissions on untrusted repository content
Invented values for fields missing from the source
Irreversible remediation taken without a human gate

hints: Each scenario has one signature trap - usually a control that got moved into a prompt.

cards.question: In the support scenario, what should escalation to a human be implemented as, rather than a phrase in the reply?
cards.answer: A tool (e.g. `escalate_to_human`) with a schema. Escalation then arrives as a typed `tool_use` block you can route, meter, and test.
hints: It should be a typed thing you can route, meter, and test.

cards.question: In the research pipeline, what should each worker return to the orchestrator instead of raw source text?
cards.answer: A compact structured summary with citations. That is what preserves the orchestrator's context window.
